introduction.text: **Before you start.** Bread is four ingredients (flour, water, salt and yeast) and a great deal of time. What turns them into a loaf with a crackling crust and an open, chewy crumb is control of two living processes:

items.text: **fermentation:** yeast producing gas and flavour;
**gluten development:** the protein network that holds the gas.

introduction.text: Home bread mostly fails because the baker follows the clock instead of the dough, or bakes without the steam and heat that make a crust. This course takes a lean dough through every stage: mixing to a target temperature, bulk fermentation read by rise and feel, shaping with tension, proofing with the poke test, and baking with steam in a home oven. It ends with a soft enriched dough and a weekday bake that fits around work.
*The log is the main tool.* Every bake records:

items.text: the formula in baker's percentages (`BAK-2`);
the dough temperature;
the times and the room temperature;
your estimates against the readings;
photos of each stage and the crumb.

introduction.text: From it you'll see how temperature and time shape your bread, in your kitchen.
*Safety* (assessment §9 and `HEA-2`): a preheated pot or stone is about 250 °C, and steam burns. Dry oven gloves on both hands, the loaf lowered in on baking paper, and water never near hot glass.

Plan about four weeks, mostly weekend baking, with short weekday tasks once the overnight retard is learned. A lean loaf takes about 5 hours from mixing to baking, mostly waiting. The loaves are the household's bread.

**Have ready:** the scale and the precision scale; bread flour (*broodmeel*) and instant yeast; a straight-sided dough container with tape to mark the rise; a bench scraper; a proofing basket or a bowl with a floured tea towel; rice flour for dusting; a razor blade or lame; the casserole of `HEA-2` with a lid; a baking stone or steel (optional) and a sheet pan for water; two dry, thick oven gloves; the probe; the oven thermometer; a wire rack; the bread log.

note.text: **Knowledge check:** the 8 items of `BRD-2.M1` in the course file. Pass mark 80 %.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** yeast is alive, and the dough's temperature sets its pace. Once you understand that, the times in a recipe stop being rules and become a guess for one kitchen, and you can read your own dough instead.

**You need:** 150 g of bread flour, 100 g of water, 3 g of salt and 1 g of instant yeast; three identical straight-sided containers or jars, marked with tape; a warm spot (near, not on, a radiator); the fridge; the phone.
**Explanation:**
*Yeast* is a living fungus that eats sugars from the flour and produces carbon dioxide (the rise), and alcohol and acids (the flavour) (`SCI-2.M6.L1`).
*The forms:*
A formula with 1 % instant yeast needs about 3 % fresh. This course uses instant yeast.
*Temperature and time:*

items.text: yeast works fastest at about 30–35 °C, slowly in the fridge, and dies at around 55–60 °C;
a dough at 24–26 °C ferments steadily;
the cooler and longer the fermentation, the more flavour, because acids and aromatic compounds build up while the gas does.

blocks.text: That is why bakers use less yeast and more time, or an overnight rest in the fridge.
*Salt* at about 2 % slows the yeast and tightens the gluten. A dough without salt rises fast and tastes flat. Weighed into the flour, not poured straight onto the yeast in a small bowl.
*Sugar* in small amounts feeds the yeast, but large amounts (enriched doughs, `BRD-2.M4`) slow it, because sugar draws water away from the yeast.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Yeast at three temperatures (40 min, then 2 hours of watching).** Mix the small dough, divide it into three equal pieces and press each into a marked container: one in the fridge, one at room temperature, one somewhere warm. Photograph all three every 30 minutes, and note the room temperature.

blocks.text: **Look for:** the warm dough doubles fastest and the fridge dough barely moves, and you can explain why.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Water hot enough to kill the yeast
Lukewarm water; the probe if unsure
Salt poured onto the yeast in a small bowl
An underrisen dough at the stated time
Following the clock in a cold kitchen
Read the dough; log the room temperature

blocks.text: **Safety:** none specific. The fridge dough is kept covered and away from ready-to-eat food.
**Record:** the photo series and two sentences explaining it, for `BRD-2.M1.X1`.

**Why it matters:** gluten is the net that holds the gas. Too little, and the loaf is flat and dense; developed well, it rises tall with an open crumb. There are three ways to build it, and the windowpane test tells you when it is done.
**You need:** 250 g of bread flour, 170 g of water, 5 g of salt, 2 g of instant yeast; a clean bench; a bench scraper; a timer; the phone.
**Explanation:**
*Gluten* forms when the proteins of wheat flour (glutenin and gliadin) take up water and are worked (`SCI-2.M3.L2`):

items.text: **glutenin** gives strength and elasticity: the dough springs back;
**gliadin** gives extensibility: the dough stretches.

blocks.text: Together they make a net that holds the gas of fermentation. Rye forms almost no such net, and spelt's is weaker and more fragile than wheat's: those flours need other handling (`BRD-3`).
*Three ways to develop it:*

items.text: **kneading,** by hand for about 10 minutes, or by mixer: fast and thorough. Push the dough away with the heel of your hand, fold it back, turn it a quarter, and repeat. It turns from shaggy to smooth and elastic;
***autolyse*:** flour and water mixed and rested for 20–60 minutes before the salt and yeast go in. The gluten starts to form without work, and the dough becomes easier to handle;

**stretch and fold:** every 30 minutes during bulk fermentation, lift one side of the dough with a wet hand, stretch it up, and fold it over the rest; turn the container and repeat from four sides. Time does most of the work, and wetter doughs can be handled.

blocks.text: *Sticky dough.* A dough is sticky at first. Don't add flour while kneading until it is stiff: use the scraper, and wet or lightly oiled hands. As the gluten develops, it stops sticking.

*The windowpane test:* tear off a small piece of dough and stretch it slowly between your fingers, turning it. A well-developed dough stretches into a thin, translucent sheet without tearing. A dough that tears at once needs more work, or more time.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Knead and test (40 min).** Knead the small dough by hand; do the windowpane test after 3, 6 and 10 minutes, and photograph each against the light. Then let the dough rise and bake it as a small loaf or rolls, or use it in `BRD-2.M1.X1`.

blocks.text: **Look for:** the dough turning from shaggy to smooth and elastic; a windowpane without tearing.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: A stiff, dry dough and a tight crumb
Adding flour while kneading until the dough is stiff
Stopping at a smooth surface without testing
A dough that tears, whatever you do
Expecting gluten from rye or spelt to behave like wheat
Bread flour here; rye and spelt in `BRD-3`

blocks.text: **Safety:** none specific.
**Record:** the three windowpane photos.

exercises.title: Kneaded against stretch-and-fold
exercises.description: The same dough kneaded versus stretch-and-fold.

blocks.text: **Task:** compare two ways of developing gluten in the same dough, and explain gluten and fermentation from the result. One batch is split in two: one half kneaded for 10 minutes, the other developed by four sets of stretch and fold. Both ferment at the same temperature, are shaped alike and baked together. Photograph the windowpanes of both halves.

**You need:** 1 kg of bread flour, 20 g of salt, 7 g of instant yeast, about 680 g of water; two straight-sided containers, marked; the probe; two loaf tins or a sheet pan; the oven thermometer; the photos of `BRD-2.M1.L1`.
**Recipe:** the lean dough in two halves.

items.text: **Mix** the flour and water until no dry flour remains, then the salt and yeast. Probe the dough and log it, with the room temperature.
**Split** it into two equal halves by weight; label them A and B.
**A, kneaded:** knead for 10 minutes; windowpane test and photo; into its container.
**B, folded:** straight into its container; four sets of stretch and fold, every 30 minutes; windowpane test and photo after the last set.
**Ferment** both side by side until risen by about half to three quarters (`BRD-2.M2.L2`); log the times.
**Shape** both alike, as loaves for the tins or as rounds on the sheet pan; proof until the poke test says ready.
**Bake** together, at your oven table's bread setting or about 230 °C, until deep golden; probe the cores (at least 93 °C).
**Cool** for an hour; cut and photograph the crumbs side by side.
**Write** the explanation: gluten developed by work and by time; and how temperature and time drove the fermentation, with the photos of `BRD-2.M1.L1`.

blocks.text: **Show:**

items.text: **`SC-STRC` level 3, the dough part:** a dough developed two ways, with the windowpanes and crumbs photographed and explained.
**`IN-BAK` level 3, the bread part:** a comparison in one formula, in cross-section, explained; the yeast and fermentation items at 80 %.
**`SC-MICR` level 3, the fermentation part:** the scenario items at 80 %, and a written explanation of how temperature and time control the yeast.

blocks.text: AI review scores the crumb photos: *competent* is two risen loaves with even crumbs and an explanation that matches them; *not yet* is a dense, unrisen half, or halves treated differently after the development.
**Time:** 1 h active, about 4 h in total.

items.question: What does yeast produce that makes bread rise?
A formula calls for 7 g of instant yeast. About how much fresh yeast do you use?
Your kitchen is 18 °C and the dough has barely risen after the time in the recipe. What do you do?
items.answer: Give it more time, or move it somewhere warmer (about 24–26 °C); read the dough, not the clock; next time use warmer water to reach the target dough temperature.

items.question: Why does a dough fermented overnight in the fridge taste better?

options.text: slow, cool fermentation builds more acids and aroma

items.question: What does salt do in bread dough?

options.text: flavours it, slows the yeast and tightens the gluten

items.why: A saltless dough rises fast and tastes flat.

items.question: What is an *autolyse*?

options.text: flour and water mixed and rested before salt and yeast, so gluten starts to form without work

items.question: What shows a dough is well developed?

options.text: it stretches into a thin, translucent windowpane without tearing

items.question: Why does stretch and fold suit a wet dough?

options.text: it develops gluten over time with little handling, which a sticky dough can't take by kneading

items.why: Time and folds instead of work.

note.text: **Knowledge check:** the 8 items of `BRD-2.M2` in the course file. Pass mark 80 %.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** a dough mixed at the right temperature ferments in a predictable time, so your notes from one bake help the next. Weighing and probing take two minutes, and they make every bake after them comparable.

**You need:** the bread formula you scaled in `BAK-2.M1.X1`, or 500 g of bread flour, 340 g of water, 10 g of salt and 4 g of instant yeast; the scale and the precision scale; the probe; a straight-sided container; a bench scraper; the bread log.
**Explanation:**
*The lean formula* in baker's percentages (`BAK-2.M1.L1`):

items.text: bread flour 100 %;
water 65–70 %;
salt 2 %;
instant yeast 0.5–1 %.

blocks.text: The 500 g above is 100 %, 68 %, 2 % and 0.8 %.
*Hydration:*

items.text: **lower (60–65 %):** a firmer dough that is easier to shape, with a tighter crumb;
**higher (70–75 %):** a slacker, stickier dough, with a more open crumb.

blocks.text: Wholemeal flour takes more water, because the bran absorbs it. Start at 68 % with white bread flour, and change it by one variable at a time in `BRD-2.M2.X1`.

*The target dough temperature:* about 24–26 °C after mixing. You control it with the water: warmer water in a cold kitchen, cooler in a warm one. Probe the dough after mixing and log the water, the room and the dough temperatures. After two or three bakes you'll know which water gives 24–26 °C in your kitchen in each season, and the bulk fermentation times become comparable.
*Mixing:*

items.text: Flour and water first, until no dry flour remains. Optionally rest it for 20–60 minutes (*autolyse*, `BRD-2.M1.L2`).
Add the yeast and salt, sprinkled over, and squeeze and fold them through with a wet hand until evenly mixed.
Develop the gluten by kneading or by folds during the bulk.

blocks.text: *Weighing.* Flour is weighed, never scooped: a scooped cup packs a different amount every time. Yeast and salt go on the precision scale.
*Sticky dough.* A 68 % dough is sticky. Work it with a wet hand and the scraper, rather than adding flour, which changes the hydration you set.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Mix and log (40 min, then 3 hours' fermentation).** Weigh the formula; choose the water temperature from the room temperature; mix; probe the dough; record everything. Carry the dough on through `BRD-2.M2.L2`.

blocks.text: **Look for:** a dough at the target temperature; all the weights in the log; a dough that feels as you expected for its hydration.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Times that never match the last bake
A stiff dough and a tight crumb
Adding flour to a sticky dough instead of using wet hands and a scraper

blocks.text: **Safety:** none specific.
**Record:** the first full entry in the bread log.

**Why it matters:** most of the flavour and strength of a loaf develop in the first rise. Shape it too early and the loaf is dense; too late and it spreads and tastes sour. The dough shows you when, if you learn to read it.

**You need:** the dough of `BRD-2.M2.L1` in a straight-sided container, marked with tape at its starting level; a bowl of water for your hand; the probe; a timer; the bread log; for session 2, two more doughs of the same formula.
**Explanation:**
*Bulk fermentation* is the first rise, from mixing to shaping.
*Folds.* Two to four sets of stretch and fold in the first half of the bulk, about every 30 minutes, build strength. After the last set, leave the dough alone.
*Reading readiness instead of the clock:*

items.text: **the rise:** about 50–75 % for a lean dough with folds, read against the tape in a straight-sided container (mark +50 % and +75 % before you start);
**bubbles** on the surface and at the sides;
**the feel:** a domed top, airy and jiggly when the container is shaken, pulling away from the sides.

blocks.text: At 24–26 °C this takes about 2–3 hours with 1 % yeast. A cooler dough takes longer; a warmer one, shorter.
*Estimate, then read* (`JD-CUES`). Every time you check:

items.text: estimate the rise from the look and feel, and write it down;
then read the tape and write the reading;
before probing the dough, estimate its temperature by touch, then probe.

blocks.text: The log shows your estimates growing more accurate. Within ±10 % for the rise and ±2 °C for the temperature counts as within tolerance.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Folds and a marked container (60 min over 3 hours).** Four sets of folds, photographed; the rise estimated, then read, every 30 minutes.
**Under and over (45 min over a day).** Two more doughs: one shaped at about 25 % rise, one at about 100 %. Bake both with a dough shaped at the right point; compare the three crumbs.

blocks.text: **Look for:** a dough that has grown by half to three quarters; a domed top; bubbles at the sides; a jiggle when shaken.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: A dense loaf, a few big holes
No idea how far it has risen
A bowl with sloping sides, where the rise can't be read
A sour, slack dough that spreads
A dough left to triple and collapse

blocks.text: **Safety:** none specific.
**Record:** the estimate-then-reading entries and the three crumb photos.
**Why it matters:** shaping gives the loaf a taut skin that holds the gas, so it rises up instead of spreading out. It takes practice in the hands, which is why this lesson has three sessions.
**You need:** fermented dough (for two loaves per session); a bench scraper; flour and rice flour; two proofing baskets, or bowls lined with floured tea towels; a shower cap or a bag.
**Explanation:**
*Pre-shaping:*

items.text: Tip the dough onto a lightly floured surface, floured side down.
Divide it with the scraper if needed, by weight.
Round each piece loosely: fold the edges in and turn it seam side down.
Rest it for 20–30 minutes, uncovered or loosely covered (the bench rest), so the gluten relaxes and it can be shaped without tearing.

blocks.text: *Shaping a round (boule):*

items.text: Flip it floured side down, and fold the edges to the centre.
Flip it seam side down.
With both hands cupped behind it, drag it towards you in short pulls on an unfloured patch of the bench, turning it a little each time. The friction tightens the surface into a smooth skin.

blocks.text: *Shaping an oval (bâtard):*

items.text: Flatten it gently into a rough rectangle.
Fold the top third down and the bottom third up.
Roll it tightly from the top, pressing the edge in with your thumbs as you go, and seal the seam with the heel of your hand.

blocks.text: *Tension* is the aim: a taut surface holds the gas and helps the loaf rise up rather than out. Too little, and the loaf spreads; too much, and the skin tears. Use only enough flour to stop sticking, and handle the dough firmly but gently, without pressing out the gas.
*Into the basket:* seam side up, in a basket or bowl dusted with flour (rice flour sticks least). Cover it, so the skin doesn't dry.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Pre-shape and boule (45 min).** Pre-shape and shape two rounds.
**Bâtard (45 min).** Pre-shape and shape two ovals.
**Tension (40 min).** Shape one loaf loosely and one tightly; proof and bake them side by side; compare the spread.

blocks.text: **Look for:** a smooth, taut skin; a loaf that holds its shape on the bench; a sealed seam.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: The dough slides and won't tighten
Too much flour on the bench, so the dough slides and won't tighten
An unfloured patch for the final pulls
Degassing the dough by pressing too hard
Less pulling; a longer bench rest
Dough that fights back and tears

blocks.text: **Safety:** none specific.
**Record:** photos of the shaped loaves on the bench, and of the loose and tight loaves after baking.

**Why it matters:** the final rise decides whether the loaf springs in the oven or spreads. The poke test reads it in seconds; the fridge lets you choose when to bake, which is what makes bread fit a working week.
**You need:** two shaped loaves in baskets; a shower cap or bag for each; flour for your finger; the fridge; the oven, pot and gloves of `BRD-2.M3.L1`; a timer; the bread log.
**Explanation:**
*Proofing* is the final rise of the shaped loaf: at room temperature, about 1–2 hours; or in the fridge, 8–16 hours (retarding).
*The poke test.* Flour a fingertip and press it about 1 cm into the side of the loaf:

items.text: **springs back at once:** underproofed. Wait, and test again in 15–20 minutes;
**springs back slowly and partly**, leaving a small dent: ready. Bake;
**doesn't spring back:** overproofed. Bake at once; it will spread, and the score won't open much.

blocks.text: Press gently: a hard poke reads every dough as overproofed. Before each test, write your prediction (under, ready or over), then compare it with the result and, after baking, with the crumb.
*Retarding* in the fridge, covered:

items.text: slows the yeast and develops flavour;
firms the dough, so it scores more cleanly;
lets the bake fit the day.

blocks.text: The loaf is baked straight from the fridge, after a poke test. A cold dough springs back more slowly, so judge it a little more generously than a warm one.
*Covered:* a shower cap or a bag over the basket, so the skin doesn't dry, harden and crack.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Room-temperature proof (40 min over 2 hours).** Poke-test every 20 minutes with a prediction; bake at "ready"; log the times and the predictions.
**A retarded proof (40 min over two days).** Shape in the evening, proof overnight in the fridge; poke-test in the morning; bake straight from the fridge.

blocks.text: **Look for:** a slow, partial spring-back, matched against the bake.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Waiting for a dough that is already overproofed
Bake at once; test earlier next time

blocks.text: **Safety:** the raw dough is kept covered in the fridge, apart from ready-to-eat food; the oven safety of `BRD-2.M3.L1` applies to every bake.
**Record:** the poke-test predictions and results against the two bakes.

exercises.title: A lean white loaf, three times
exercises.description: A lean white loaf, three times over three weeks.

blocks.text: **Task:** carry a lean dough through every stage with a guiding recipe, three times over three weeks, reading the dough instead of the clock. Change one thing per bake, written in advance: the hydration, the shape (*boule* or *bâtard*), or room proof against retard. Log the times and every estimate, then its reading.

**You need:** per bake: 500 g of bread flour, about 340 g of water, 10 g of salt, 4 g of instant yeast; the container and tape; the probe; a basket; the casserole; gloves; a blade; the bread log. The loaves are the household's bread.
**Recipe:** a lean loaf (100 % flour, 68 % water, 2 % salt, 0.8 % yeast).

items.text: **Weigh, mix and probe:** water chosen for a dough of 24–26 °C; estimate, then probe.
**Bulk:** four sets of folds in the first two hours; estimate, then read the rise every 30 minutes; shape at 50–75 %.
**Pre-shape**, rest 20–30 minutes, and **shape**; into the basket, covered.
**Proof** at room temperature, or overnight in the fridge; poke-test with a prediction.
**Preheat** the casserole with the lid in the oven at about 250 °C for 45 minutes; check the thermometer.
**Score** the loaf on a sheet of baking paper; lower it into the pot by the paper, with dry gloves; lid on.
**Bake** 20 minutes with the lid on; then lid off, at about 230 °C, until deep brown, about 20–25 minutes more.
**Predict** doneness by colour and sound, then probe the core through the base: at least 93 °C.
**Cool** on a rack for at least an hour; cut and photograph the dough at each stage, the crust and the crumb.

blocks.text: **Show:**

items.text: **`TS-BRD` level 2:** a lean loaf from a formula, risen, baked through with the core at least 93 °C, and an even crumb, three times.
**`JD-CUES` level 3, the dough part:** at least ten estimate-then-reading entries over the three bakes, at least eight within tolerance (±2 °C for temperatures, ±10 % for the rise).

blocks.text: AI review scores the crumb against the reference images: *competent* is an even crumb without dense patches, risen, with an "ear" at the score; *not yet* is a dense, gummy crumb or a large hole under the crust, a flat, spread loaf, or a pale crust. The rubric: risen, even crumb without gummy patches, crust deep golden (each yes or no).
**Time:** 3 × about 1.25 h active over 5 hours.

items.question: A dough of 500 g of flour at 68 % hydration needs how much water?
What does a higher hydration give?

options.text: a firmer dough and tighter crumb
a slacker dough and a more open crumb

items.question: Why is the dough temperature probed after mixing?

options.text: fermentation speed depends on it, so the times become predictable and comparable

items.question: How do you know bulk fermentation is done?

options.text: the dough has grown by about half to three quarters, is domed, bubbly at the sides and jiggles

items.question: Your loaf is dense and tight, with a few big holes under the crust. What happened, and what do you change?
items.answer: Underfermented (bulk or proof too short, or too cold); give it more time or a warmer spot, and judge by rise and the poke test.

items.question: Why build tension when shaping?

options.text: a taut skin holds the gas so the loaf rises up rather than spreading

items.question: You poke a proofing loaf and the dent springs back at once. What does it mean?
items.why: A slow, partial spring-back means ready.

items.question: What does retarding a shaped loaf in the fridge do?

options.text: slows fermentation, develops flavour, firms the dough for scoring and fits the bake to the day

items.why: The fridge is a planning tool.

note.text: **Knowledge check:** the 8 items of `BRD-2.M3` in the course file, 2 of them safety items. Pass mark 80 %, with every safety item correct.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** a home oven is dry, and a loaf baked dry stays small and dull. With steam, the same dough springs and bakes a glossy crust. At these heats, loading the oven safely is part of the skill.

**You need:** two shaped loaves; the casserole of `HEA-2` with a lid and a metal or ovenproof knob; a baking stone or steel, or a sheet pan; a second sheet pan or tray for water; a kettle; baking paper; two dry, thick oven gloves; the oven thermometer; the calibration log.
**Explanation:**
*Oven spring.* In the first 10–15 minutes of baking, the gas in the loaf expands and the yeast makes a last burst, until the crust sets. A loaf can grow by a third.

*Why steam.* Moisture on the surface keeps the crust soft and stretchy, so the loaf can spring fully. It also gelatinises the surface starch, for a glossy, crackling crust. Without steam, the crust sets early and the loaf stays small, with a dull, thick crust.
*Three ways at home:*

items.text: **a Dutch oven** (the casserole), preheated with the oven, lid on for the first 20 minutes: the loaf's own moisture is the steam. It is the simplest and the most reliable;
**a baking stone or steel,** preheated for 45 minutes, with a tray of boiling water on the shelf below for the first 15 minutes;
**a tray of water** in a plain oven, with the loaf on a preheated sheet pan: the weakest of the three.

blocks.text: *Heat.* A lean loaf bakes at about 230–250 °C, checked with the oven thermometer (`EQP-1`), then lower once the steam is gone. Log the real temperature and the preheat time of the pot or stone (`KM-EQPT`).
*Loading safely:*

items.text: a preheated pot or stone is about 250 °C: dry oven gloves go on both hands, because a damp glove passes heat straight through as steam;
the loaf goes in on a sheet of baking paper, lowered by its corners, so your hands stay out of the pot;
lift the lid away from you, so the steam rises on the far side;
pour boiling water into the preheated tray with your arm clear of the steam;
water never touches a hot stone, the oven glass or the door, which can crack.

blocks.text: **Practice:**

items.text: **Dutch oven (50 min over a bake).** Preheat the pot; load the loaf safely; bake lid on, then lid off; photograph the spring at the moment the lid comes off and at the end.
**Stone or tray (50 min over a bake).** The second loaf with the other method; compare the spring and the crust.

blocks.text: **Look for:** a loaf that grows and opens at the score; a glossy, deep crust; the oven temperature logged against the dial.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: A flat loaf, a pale base
Preheat it with the oven, 45 minutes
A cracked oven door or stone
Water only into the preheated tray
A small loaf, a closed score
Dry, thick gloves on both hands

blocks.text: **Safety:** the module's safety items are the loading rules above: dry gloves, paper, the lid away from you, and water never on hot glass or stone.
**Record:** the oven reading and preheat times in the calibration log; the photos of both loaves.

**Why it matters:** a cut decides where the loaf opens as it springs, instead of bursting at a weak point; and the colour of the crust is most of its flavour. Most home bakers score too timidly and pull their loaves too pale.
**You need:** shaped loaves, ideally retarded in the fridge; a razor blade or lame, or a sharp serrated knife; baking paper; the casserole or stone; dry gloves; the phone.
**Explanation:**
*Why score.* As the loaf springs in the oven, the skin has to give somewhere. A cut controls where it opens, so the loaf expands evenly and keeps its shape.
*How to score:*

items.text: for an oval, hold the blade at a shallow angle, about 30° to the surface, and make one long cut along the length, slightly off-centre: the flap lifts into an "ear";
for a round, cut straight down: a cross, or a square;
make each cut one quick, confident stroke, about 0.5–1 cm deep;
a cold, retarded dough scores most cleanly, because it is firm.

blocks.text: Score just before loading, on the baking paper, and load at once.

*Baking to colour.* Bake the crust to a deep golden brown, with darker edges at the score, past where a beginner would stop. The colour is flavour (`SC-BRWN`), and a pale crust softens as the loaf cools, because there is still moisture in it. If the top colours too fast, lower the heat rather than taking the loaf out early.
*Listen.* A well-baked lean loaf crackles as it cools on the rack: the crust is contracting.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Score (40 min).** On shaped dough, practise single slashes, a cross and a square; bake them and photograph how each opened.
**Colour (40 min).** Bake two loaves: pull one at light golden, the other at deep brown. Compare the crust after an hour, by touch, sound and taste.

blocks.text: **Look for:** a clean, open score with an ear; a deep, even brown crust that crackles as it cools.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: A torn, ragged cut that doesn't open
A loaf that bursts at the side, or a gaping, flat cut
Scoring too deep or too shallow

blocks.text: **Safety:** the blade is stored with its cover on. Scoring happens before loading, never over the hot pot.
**Record:** the score photos and the two crusts side by side.

**Why it matters:** a loaf can look done and still be gummy inside. Colour, sound and weight give you a good guess; the probe confirms it. And once it is cut, the crumb tells you what happened in the bulk and the proof.
**You need:** two loaves at the end of baking; the probe; a wire rack; a bread knife; the bread log with the bakes' times; the phone.
**Explanation:**
*The cues of a done loaf:*

items.text: a deep crust colour;
a hollow sound when the base is tapped;
a loaf that feels light for its size.

blocks.text: Write your prediction (done or not), then confirm it with the probe: the core of a lean loaf is at least 93 °C (the `TS-BRD` level 2 standard). Probe through the base or the side into the centre, not through the score, where the crust is thin and the reading is misleading. If it is short, it goes back in the oven for 5 minutes, directly on the shelf.
*Cooling.* The crumb is still setting as steam escapes, so a loaf cools on a rack for at least an hour before cutting. A loaf cut hot is gummy, however well it was baked.
*Reading a crumb.* Cut through the centre and photograph the face:

rows: Dense, tight, a few big holes under the crust
Large irregular holes, a flat loaf that spread
Even, with a mix of small and medium holes
As intended for a lean white loaf

blocks.text: *Check the log before you blame anything.* A dense crumb from a log that shows a cold dough and a short bulk points at the fermentation, not the flour. As in `BAK-2.M4.L3`: one fault, one change next time.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Predict and probe (30 min).** For two loaves, predict doneness by colour and sound, then probe; cool, cut, and read each crumb against the table and the log.

blocks.text: **Look for:** predictions that match the probe; a crumb diagnosis that matches the log.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Through the base, into the centre
A gummy crumb in a done loaf
Blaming the flour without reading the log

blocks.text: **Safety:** the loaf is lifted out of the pot with dry gloves; the probe is cleaned after use.
**Record:** the predictions and probe readings (doneness entries for `JD-CUES`), and the crumb diagnoses.

exercises.title: Two steam methods
exercises.description: The lean loaf baked with two steam methods; crumb photos.

blocks.text: **Task:** bake the lean loaf with two steam methods from a framework, compare the spring, the crust and the crumb, and log the oven and the doneness readings. One dough makes two loaves: one in the Dutch oven, the other on a stone, steel or preheated sheet pan with a tray of water.
**You need:** 1 kg of bread flour, 20 g of salt, about 7 g of instant yeast, water; two baskets; the casserole; a stone or pan and a water tray; dry gloves; the thermometers; the calibration log.
**Framework:** two steam methods.

rows: The lean formula, 65–70 % water, mixed to 24–26 °C, folded, shaped as two loaves
The thermometer at the baking setting; the preheat time of the pot and the stone logged
In the preheated pot, lid on for 20 minutes, then off
On the preheated stone or pan, boiling water in the tray below for the first 15 minutes
About 230–250 °C with steam, lower once the steam is gone
When to lower; when it is deep brown
On baking paper, dry gloves on both hands, lid away from you, water never on glass
Colour and sound predicted, then the core probed: at least 93 °C

blocks.text: *Procedure:*

items.text: Mix, ferment and shape.
Log the oven reading and the preheat times.
Bake both loaves, safely loaded, one after the other if the oven holds only one method at a time.
Predict, then probe each core.
Cool for an hour.
Photograph the crust, the score and the crumb of each, side by side.
Write which method to use from now on, and why.

blocks.text: **Show:**

items.text: **`TS-BRD` level 2:** the loaves risen with oven spring, a deep crust, the core at least 93 °C, an even crumb.

**`KM-EQPT` level 3, the bread-oven part:** the oven reading and preheat times in the calibration log; the cast-iron pot kept seasoned and rust-free. With `BAK-2.M1.X1`, `HEA-2` and `KNF-2`, the row is complete.
**`JD-CUES` level 3:** the doneness entries, added to those of `BRD-2.M2.X1`.

blocks.text: AI review scores the crumb and crust photos as in `BRD-2.M2.X1`.
**Time:** 1.25 h active, about 5 hours in total.

items.question: Why is steam used in the first part of baking bread?

options.text: it keeps the crust soft so the loaf can spring, and gives a glossy crust

items.question: Why is a lidded Dutch oven a good steam method at home?

options.text: the loaf's own moisture is trapped as steam under the lid

items.question: You load a loaf into a preheated Dutch oven. What is safe?

options.text: a damp tea towel as a glove
dry oven gloves on both hands, the loaf lowered in on baking paper
dropping it in from a height

items.why: The pot is around 250 °C; wet cloth conducts heat.

items.question: Where do you pour water for steam in a plain oven?

options.text: into a preheated tray on a lower shelf, away from glass and stone

items.why: Water cracks hot glass and stone.

items.question: Why score a loaf?

options.text: to control where it opens during oven spring

items.why: Otherwise it bursts at a weak point.

items.question: What is the core temperature of a done lean loaf?
Your loaf is gummy inside, though it looked well browned. Name two possible causes.
items.answer: Underbaked (core below 93 °C), or cut before it had cooled for an hour.

items.question: A loaf spread flat with large irregular holes. Most likely cause?

options.text: overproofed, or too little tension in shaping

items.why: Read the crumb against the log.

note.text: **Knowledge check:** the 8 items of `BRD-2.M4` in the course file. Pass mark 80 %.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** soft rolls and milk bread are everyday Dutch bread (*zachte bolletjes*, *krentenbollen*), and they behave quite differently from a lean dough. Knowing why lets you adjust the timing and the oven instead of being surprised by them.

**You need:** the soft-roll formula of `BRD-2.M4.X1`; the mixer (optional); a sheet pan or the loaf tin of `BAK-2`; baking paper; an egg for the wash and a pastry brush; the probe; the oven thermometer.
**Explanation:**
*Enriched doughs* add fat (butter), sugar, milk and often egg. Examples are milk bread, soft rolls, *krentenbollen* and, richer still, brioche (in `BRD-3`).
*What the enrichments do:*

items.text: **fat** coats the gluten and tenderises the crumb, giving a soft, fine texture and a soft crust. It gets in the way of gluten forming, so it is added after some gluten has developed: knead the dough first, then work in the soft butter a piece at a time;
**sugar** slows the yeast (it draws water away) and browns the crust faster;
**milk** softens the crumb and colours the crust;
**egg** adds richness, colour and structure.

blocks.text: *The consequences:*

items.text: a slower rise: more yeast, or more time, and the dough is read by its rise, not the lean dough's timing;
a lower baking temperature, about 180–190 °C, so the crust doesn't burn before the inside is done;
a lower core temperature at done: about 88–90 °C.

blocks.text: *Tangzhong* (optional): a little of the flour cooked with some of the milk into a thick paste, cooled and added to the dough. It holds more water, and keeps the bread soft for days.

*Shaping rolls.* Divide the dough by weight, so every roll bakes in the same time. Round each piece under a cupped hand on an unfloured surface, moving your hand in small circles until it forms a tight ball. Set them close together on the pan, so they rise into each other and bake with soft sides. Proof them covered, then egg-wash for a shine.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Soft rolls (75 min active, about 4 hours in total).** Mix; knead; add the butter once the gluten has started; ferment; divide by weight; shape; proof; egg-wash and bake; probe; cool and photograph the crumb.

blocks.text: **Look for:** a smooth, soft, slightly tacky dough; rolls of equal size; a shiny, golden crust; a soft, fine crumb.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: A dough that stays greasy and won't develop
Butter added at the start, so the dough won't develop
A dough fermented on the lean timing
Read the rise; allow more time
A dark crust, a doughy inside
A dark crust from a lean bread's oven heat

blocks.text: **Safety:** the egg wash is raw egg: the brush and bowl are washed after use, and the rolls are baked through (core about 88–90 °C).
**Record:** the dough temperature and times, for comparison with the lean dough.

exercises.title: Soft rolls or a milk loaf
exercises.description: Soft rolls or a milk loaf.

blocks.text: **Task:** make a soft enriched bread with a guiding recipe, and compare its behaviour with the lean dough. Choose rolls (weighed pieces) or a milk loaf in the loaf tin of `BAK-2`. Log the dough temperature and the times, for comparison with your lean bakes.

**You need:** 500 g of bread flour; 270 g of milk; 50 g of soft butter; 40 g of sugar; an egg, and another for the wash; 7 g of instant yeast; 9 g of salt; a sheet pan or the loaf tin; the probe; the scale.
**Recipe:** soft rolls (12) or a milk loaf. In baker's percentages: flour 100 %, milk 54 %, egg 10 %, butter 10 %, sugar 8 %, yeast 1.4 %, salt 1.8 %.

items.text: **Mix** the flour, sugar, yeast and salt; add the lukewarm milk and the egg; mix until no dry flour remains.
**Develop:** knead for about 8 minutes, until smooth.
**Add the butter** a piece at a time, kneading until each disappears and the dough is smooth and slightly tacky; a windowpane should stretch thin. Probe and log the dough.
**Ferment** covered until about doubled, logging the rise against the tape; expect it to be slower than the lean dough.
**Divide** by weight into 12 pieces (about 75 g each), and round them; or shape one loaf as a *bâtard* for the tin.
**Proof** covered, close together on the pan or in the tin, until puffy and the poke test is slow.
**Egg-wash** and bake at about 180–190 °C until golden: rolls about 15–20 minutes, a loaf longer.
**Probe** the core: about 88–90 °C.
**Cool** on a rack; cut and photograph the crumb.
**Write** three differences from the lean dough, with the reason for each.

blocks.text: **Show:** **`TS-BRD` level 2:** the enriched bread risen and baked through (about 88–90 °C at the core); even rolls or an even loaf; a soft, fine crumb in cross-section; and the differences from the lean dough explained.
AI review scores the crumb and tray photos: *competent* is even, golden rolls with a soft, fine crumb; *not yet* is uneven sizes, a dark crust, or a dense or doughy crumb.
**Time:** 1.25 h active, about 4 hours in total.

items.question: Why does an enriched dough rise more slowly than a lean one?

options.text: sugar draws water away from the yeast, and fat coats the gluten

items.question: When is the butter added to an enriched dough?
Why are soft rolls baked at a lower temperature than a lean loaf?

options.text: sugar, milk and egg brown quickly, so the crust would burn

items.question: What does fat do to the crumb?

options.text: tenderises it into a soft, fine texture

items.question: Why are soft rolls weighed before shaping?

options.text: so they are equal in size and bake evenly

items.question: Why are rolls set close together on the tray?

options.text: they rise into each other and stay soft-sided

items.question: What is *tangzhong*?

options.text: a cooked flour-and-milk paste that holds more water and keeps bread soft

items.question: Your enriched dough has barely risen after the time a lean dough takes. What do you do?
items.answer: Give it more time (enriched doughs are slower), in a warm spot; judge by the rise and the poke test, not the clock.

note.text: **Knowledge check:** none for this module. Its only judgment objective, reviewing the log, is shown in the review rather than by scenario items; scheduling with the fridge was checked in `BRD-2.M2`.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** a loaf takes five hours, but only about one of them is work. With the fridge as a pause button, fresh bread fits around a working day, if you plan backwards and check the dough at the right points.
**You need:** your diary for the coming week; the bread log of the course; the backwards-schedule template (`WRK-1.M2.L3`); the journal.
**Explanation:**
*The fridge as a pause button.* A dough can be slowed at two points:

items.text: **after mixing:** a cold bulk fermentation;
**after shaping:** a retarded proof.

blocks.text: So a loaf can be mixed in the evening, shaped the next evening and baked the morning after. Or it can be mixed in the morning, shaped after work, retarded overnight and baked before work.
*A backwards schedule* (`KM-PLAN`, `WRK-1.M2.L3`):

items.text: Start from when the bread should come out of the oven.
Work back through cooling, baking, preheating, proofing, shaping, bulk and mixing, with a time for each.
Mark the control points: the dough temperature after mixing, the rise before shaping, the poke test before baking.
Mark the parallel tasks around the working day: dinner cooked during the bulk, for example.

blocks.text: An example for a weekday: mix at 18:00 and cook dinner during the folds; shape at 21:00 at 50–75 % rise; into the fridge; preheat at 06:15; bake at 07:00 from the fridge; cool while you get ready; bread on the table that evening.

*The plan against the actual.* Each stage gets a planned and an actual time. Where the dough wasn't ready, write the change and the reason: "bulk 45 minutes longer: dough below 24 °C, kitchen cold". A schedule that ignores the kitchen temperature will be wrong in winter.
*The bread log review,* as in `BAK-2.M6.L2`. Read the course's bakes for patterns:

items.text: fermentation times against dough temperature;
crumb faults against proofing;
your own banding against the AI review and the tasters.

blocks.text: Then set two or three specific targets for `BRD-3`.
**Practice:**

items.text: **The schedule (45 min).** Write a two-day schedule for a weekday bake, with control points and parallel tasks.
**The review (45 min, after the bake).** Set plan against actual; read the log; mark the agreements; write the targets.

blocks.text: **Look for:** a schedule that fits around work; every control point with a reading; a review that cites entries and photos.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: The dough isn't ready on time
A schedule that ignores the kitchen temperature
Plan from the logged times at that temperature

blocks.text: **Safety:** none specific; the oven safety of `BRD-2.M3.L1` applies to an early-morning bake too.
**Record:** the schedule, the plan-against-actual log and the review (in `BRD-2.M5.X1`).

exercises.title: A weekday bake with an overnight retard
exercises.description: A weekday bake planned with an overnight retard.

blocks.text: **Task:** plan a lean loaf around a working day with an overnight retard, follow the plan with control points, and review the course's bread log. Write the schedule in advance: mixing, bulk, shaping and retard on a weekday evening; baking the next morning or evening; with the control points and a parallel task (a dinner cooked during the bulk). Log the plan against the actual for every stage, with a reasoned change wherever the dough wasn't ready. For the review, take five bread entries (from `BRD-2.M2` to `BRD-2.M5`) and set your band against the AI or taster band for each.
**You need:** 500 g of bread flour, 10 g of salt, about 3 g of instant yeast, water; the dinner of the evening; the container, basket, pot, gloves and probe; the schedule template; the bread log.
**Framework:** the weekday bake.

rows: Backwards from the bake; every stage with a planned time
Dough temperature after mixing; the rise before shaping; the poke test before baking
A dinner cooked during the bulk
The shaped loaf, covered, overnight in the fridge
From the fridge, as in `BRD-2.M3.L1`; core at least 93 °C
Each stage's planned and actual time; a reason for every change
Five entries; your band against the AI or taster band; patterns; two or three targets

blocks.text: *Procedure:*

items.text: Write the schedule.
Mix, ferment and shape, logging the plan and the actual times.
Cook the dinner during the bulk.
Retard the loaf overnight.
Bake it.
Photograph the crumb.
Write the review and the targets.

blocks.text: **Show:**

items.text: **`KM-PLAN` level 3, the bread part:** your own two-day schedule with parallel tasks and control points; every stage started within 15 minutes of the plan, or changed with a reason logged.
**`JD-REFL` level 3:** five bread-log entries where your band agrees with the AI or the tasters within one band in at least four, with the review and the targets for `BRD-3`.

blocks.text: AI review scores the crumb photo as in `BRD-2.M2.X1`.
**Time:** 1.5 h active over two days.
